You will be assessed on the statistics and decoder accuracy of your converted data, and on whether an expert would consider each of your decisions well justified.\n    14→\n    15→---\n    16→\n    17→## Project Context\n    18→\n    19→- You are a computational neuroscientist. Your goal is to load and reformat data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis.\n    20→- You need to use the **SAME** processing of the data described in the provided reference paper and code repository when applicable. This requires examining the provided paper, code, and data to understand how the data is formatted and processed, and determine how to balance this with the requirements of the new downstream analysis.\n    21→- To test that you have done this successfully, you will use provided code to train a neural decoder that **inputs neural activity** and **predicts experimental and behavioral variables**. \n    22→- We will assess your work in two ways. First, statistics of the converted data and decoder accuracy will be compared to those of an expert-written solution. Second, each decision you make about how to load, filter, process, align, and save the data will be compared with the decision made by an expert. A decision that differs from the expert's is acceptable if it is equally well justified; decisions that are poorly justified will be flagged as concerning or incorrect.\n    23→\n    24→## Reference Information\n    25→\n    26→- The reference **paper** \"A flexible hippocampal population code for experience relative to reward\" is in the file `/app/paper.pdf`.\n    27→- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n    28→- **Code** from the paper are in the directory `/app/code`.\n    29→- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `/app/data`.\n    30→- **Documentation** on nwb file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io/en/latest/\n    31→\n    32→## Decoder Task\n    33→\n    34→Temporally align based on start of the trial. \n    35→\n    36→### Decoder Inputs:\n    37→- Time from start of trial in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n    38→- Environment type (binary, ENV1 vs ENV2, per trial)\n    39→- Trial number (continuous, per trial)\n    40→- Previous trial outcome (binary, omitted = 0, rewarded = 1, per trial)\n    41→\n    42→### Decoder Outputs\n    43→- Distance to any location in the reward zone, time-varying. Discretization bins:\n    44→  - 0:  < -50 cm\n    45→  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\n    46→  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\n    47→  - 3: 0 cm\n    48→  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\n    49→  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\n    50→  - 6: > +50 cm\n    51→- Absolute position in corridor, time-varying. Discretized into 5 equal-sized bins spanning the 450 cm track:\n    52→  - 0: < 90 cm\n    53→  - 1: 90 to 180 cm\n    54→  - 2: 180 to 270 cm\n    55→  - 3: 270 to 360 cm\n    56→  - 4: > 360 cm\n    57→- Speed, time-varying. Discretized into bins:\n    58→  - 0: < 2 cm/s\n    59→  - 1: 2-10 cm/s\n    60→  - 2: 10-20 cm/s\n    61→  - 3: 20-40 cm/s\n    62→  - 4: > 40 cm/s\n    63→- Lick, time-varying. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n    64→- Reward zone location, per-trial. 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C\n    65→- Reward outcome, per-trial. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n    66→\n    67→## Target Data Format\n    68→\n    69→- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n    70→- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n    71→\n    72→```python\n    73→data = {\n    74→    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n    75→        [  # list of trials for session 1\n    76→            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n    77→            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n    78→            ...\n    79→        ],\n    80→        [  # list of trials for session 2\n    81→            ...\n    82→        ],\n    83→        ...\n    84→    ],\n    85→\n    86→    'input': [  # list of sessions\n    87→        [  # list of trials for session 1\n    88→            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n    89→            ...\n    90→        ],\n    91→        ...\n    92→    ],\n    93→\n    94→    'output': [  # list of sessions\n    95→        [  # list of trials for session 1\n    96→            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n    97→            ...\n    98→        ],\n    99→        ...\n   100→    ],\n   101→\n   102→    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n   103→    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n   104→\n   105→    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n   106→    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n   107→        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n   108→    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n   109→\n   110→    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n   111→    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n   112→    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n   113→        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n   114→        ...\n   115→    ],\n   116→\n   117→    'metadata': {\n   118→        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n   119→        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n   120→        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n   121→        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n   122→        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n   123→        ...\n   124→    }\n   125→}\n   126→```\n   127→\n   128→### Key Format Requirements\n   129→\n   130→- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n   131→  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n   132→  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n   133→  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n   134→\n   135→- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n   136→  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n   137→  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n   138→    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n   139→    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n   140→    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n   141→  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n   142→  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n   143→  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n   144→\n   145→- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n   146→  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n   147→  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n   148→  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n   149→  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n   150→  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n   151→\n   152→- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n   153→- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n   154→  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n   155→\n   156→- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n   157→- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n   158→\n   159→- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n   160→  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n   161→\n   162→- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n   163→  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n   164→- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n   165→  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n   166→\n   167→- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n   168→  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n   169→  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n   170→  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n   171→  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n   172→  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n   173→\n   174→## Python environment\n   175→\n   176→- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n   177→- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n   178→- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n   179→\n   180→## Decoder Reference\n   181→\n   182→- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n   183→- Optional arguments:\n   184→  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n   185→  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n   186→  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n   187→- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n   188→\n   189→### Purpose\n   190→\n   191→These functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n   192→1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n   193→2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n   194→3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n   195→4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n   196→5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n   197→\n   198→### Consistency requirements\n   199→\n   200→Your processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\n   201→- Loading of data\n   202→- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n   203→- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n   204→- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n   205→\n   206→To check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n   207→\n   208→Whenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n   209→\n   210→Discrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n   211→\n   212→Carefully verify your work after every step. Important functions from exploring the reference code\n   312→  - Dataset structure from exploring the dataset\n   313→  - Analysis described in the reference texts\n   314→- Note and investigate any discrepancies\n   315→- In particular, look for discrepancies in:\n   316→  - Experimental and behavioral variables\n   317→  - Data processing\n   318→  - Data curation\n   319→- Iterate until your understanding of the reference code, dataset, and reference texts are consistent\n   320→\n   321→**Done when**: You have resolved all discrepancies and documented your final understanding in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 4\".\n   322→\n   323→**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 5, update Step 4 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n   324→\n   325→---\n   326→\n   327→### Step 5: Mapping Planning\n   328→\n   329→**Goal**: Create a detailed plan for mapping source data to target format.\n   330→\n   331→**Actions**:\n   332→- Map source data elements to target format components:\n   333→  - Which variables contain neural activity?\n   334→  - Identify ALL available experimental variables\n   335→  - Which variables should be decoder **inputs** vs **outputs**? (Follow Decoder Task section)\n   336→  - How to discretize continuous outputs (Follow Decoder Task section)\n   337→  - Which inputs/outputs should be **time-varying** vs **per-trial** (Follow Decoder Task section)\n   338→  - How does the reference code load and manipulate this data?\n   339→  - When possible, import or copy code from the reference code in `/app/code` directory. \n   340→- Consult CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4 and reference materials to determine:\n   341→  - Temporal binning for spike rates (if applicable)\n   342→  - Temporal alignment of trials\n   343→  - Data filtering and curation rules for neurons, trials, and sessions\n   344→  - Brain regions recorded from\n   345→- Mapping should be consistent with CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4.\n   346→- Check for variables indicating valid data periods — exclude invalid data\n   347→- Note all decisions, edge cases, and data quality issues\n   348→- Plan and document **sanity and consistency checks** based on dataset size information from the reference texts, code, and data\n   349→\n   350→**Done when**:\n   351→- You have a complete mapping document in CONVERSION_NOTES.md specifying every source-to-target variable mapping under \"Step 5\"\n   352→- You have documented all decisions under \"Step 5\"\n   353→- You have documented sanity and consistency checks under \"Step 5\"\n   354→\n   355→**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 6, update Step 5 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n   356→\n   357→---\n   358→\n   359→### Step 6: Script Development\n   360→\n   361→**Goal**: Write the conversion script to `/app/convert_data.py`.\n   362→\n   363→**Actions**:\n   364→- Write all conversion code in the file `/app/convert_data.py`\n   365→- Script should run as **`python -u /app/convert_data.py <outpicklefile>`**\n   366→- Include options:\n   367→  - `--full` (default): Process all sessions\n   368→  - `--sample`: Process only 2 sessions for testing\n   369→  - `--show-processing`: Plot visualizations of EVERY processing step for up to 2 sessions. Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\n   370→- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\n   371→- Write efficient code:\n   372→  - Vectorize loops\n   373→  - Avoid unnecessary file I/O\n   374→  - Use parallel processing if beneficial\n   375→  - Print timing information to find bottlenecks\n   376→- Plots for `--show-processing` mode should visually convince the user that every step of the conversion is correct.\n   377→  - There are no temporal misalignments\n   378→  - Discretization of continuous outputs is correct\n   379→- Write clear, well-documented functions\n   380→- Handle missing data appropriately (consult references, use sensible defaults, document)\n   381→- Validate data shapes and types at each step\n   382→- Include sanity checks (e.g., trial counts match across arrays)\n   383→\n   384→**Done when**: `/app/convert_data.py` exists and runs efficiently without errors.\n   385→\n   386→**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 7 until `/app/convert_data.py` exists and you have updated Step 6 in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n   387→\n   388→---\n   389→\n   390→### Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n   391→\n   392→**Goal**: Validate the conversion on a small sample before processing the full dataset.\n   393→\n   394→**Actions**:\n   395→1. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\n   396→  a. Verify the sample data structure matches the specification.\n   397→  b. Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\n   398→  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \n   399→  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\n   400→2. Improve efficiency of conversion.\n   401→  a. Look at and note timing information for the conversion. \n   402→  b. Estimate how long the full conversion will run. When you do this, make sure that your estimate accounts for differences in lengths/numbers of trials/sessions. \n   403→  c. If full conversion time estimate is longer than 15 minutes, speed up the code by writing more efficient code (vectorizing loops, removing unnecessary or redundant computations) and/or including parallel processing. \n   404→3. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_sample_out.txt`.\n   405→4. Analyze the output file `/app/verification_sample_out.txt`:\n   406→  a. Verify no errors reported.\n   407→  b. Attempt to address any warnings\n   408→  c. Check input ranges and output value distributions against expectations from reference texts.\n   409→\n   410→**Done when**: \n   411→- `/app/sample_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\n   412→- `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\n   413→- Processing plots show no anomalies\n   414→- Document sample statistics in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 7\"\n   415→\n   416→**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 8 until `/app/sample_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` files exist, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 7 is filled in. \n   417→\n   418→---\n   419→\n   420→### Step 8: Sample Decoder Training\n   421→\n   422→**Goal**: Verify the decoder runs successfully on sample data.\n   423→\n   424→**Actions**:\n   425→1. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl 2>&1 | tee /app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt`\n   426→2. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\n   427→3. **Check accuracy**: Verify accuracy is above chance for EVERY output\n   428→\n   429→**Investigate any issues**:\n   430→- If accuracy is low: check for conversion bugs or reconsider output representation\n   431→\n   432→**Done when**: \n   433→- Decoder training completes without errors\n   434→- Loss decreases over epochs\n   435→- Accuracies are above chance\n   436→- Document all results in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 8\"\n   437→\n   438→**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 9 until `/app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt` file exists, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 8 is filled in. \n   439→\n   440→---\n   441→\n   442→### Step 9: Full Conversion and Validation\n   443→\n   444→**Goal**: Process the complete dataset.\n   445→\n   446→**Actions**:\n   447→1. Review your time estimate from Step 7.\n   448→2. If estimated time is long (e.g. longer than 15 minutes), optimize bottlenecks first.\n   449→3. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/converted_data.pkl --full 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_full_out.txt`\n   450→4. As the code runs, update your estimates of how long processing will take. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \n   451→5. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_full_out.txt`. \n   452→6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \n   453→7. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\n   454→8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `/app/verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\n   455→9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\n   456→\n   457→**Done when**:\n   458→- `/app/converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\n   459→- `/app/verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\n   460→- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\n   461→- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 9\"\n   462→\n   463→**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `/app/converted_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\n   464→\n   465→---\n   466→\n   467→### Step 10: Critical Review 1\n   468→\n   469→**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain.\n   470→\n   471→**Check 1: Output log verification**\n   472→Read through `/app/verification_full_out.txt` to find and fix **all errors**. Address each warning by either fixing its cause or verifying it that it is not possible to fix it. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n   473→\n   474→**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\n   475→- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\n   476→- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\n   477→- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \n   478→- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \n   479→- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \n   480→- Document your sanity checks to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n   481→\n   482→**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\n   483→- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \n   484→- For each major processing step — (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction — identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \n   485→- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \n   486→- Fix any mismatches. \n   487→- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n   488→- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\n   489→\n   490→**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\n   491→- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference paper. \n   492→- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \n   493→- Fix any discovered issues. \n   494→- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n   495→\n   496→**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\n   497→- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \n   498→- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \n   499→\n   500→**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n   501→1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n   502→2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n   503→3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n   504→4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n   505→\n   506→Write a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 10\".\n   507→\n   508→**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \n   509→\n   510→---\n   511→\n   512→### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\n   513→\n   514→**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\n   515→\n   516→**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Do not skip or abbreviate. Do not proceed to Step 12 until this step is completely finished.\n   517→\n   518→**Actions**:\n   519→1. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --plot-samples 2>&1 | tee /app/train_decoder_full_out.txt`. If the GPU does not have sufficient RAM for the network training, use the flag `--cpu` to specify to use the CPU to train. \n   520→2. **Wait for complete execution** — this may take significant time for large datasets\n   521→3. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\n   522→4. **Check accuracy**: High accuracy is an indicator that data conversion has been done correctly. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the paper. \n   523→\n   524→**Done when**: \n   525→1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\n   526→2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 11\" with a table of accuracies\n   527→\n   528→---\n   529→\n   530→### Step 12: Critical Review 2\n   531→\n   532→**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\n   533→\n   534→**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n   535→- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n   536→- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n   537→- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n   538→\n   539→**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\n   540→- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\n   541→- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\n   542→- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n   543→- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n   544→\n   545→**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n   546→- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n   547→\n   548→**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n   549→1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n   550→2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n   551→3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n   552→4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n   553→5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \n   554→\n   555→**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n   556→1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n   557→2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n   558→3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n   559→4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n   560→\n   561→**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n   562→\n   563→**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n   564→\n   565→---\n   566→\n   567→### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n   568→\n   569→**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n   570→\n   571→**Actions**:\n   572→- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n   573→  - Key decisions and rationale\n   574→  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n   575→  - Validation results and tables\n   576→  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n   577→- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n   578→  - Dataset description\n   579→  - How to load and use the converted data\n   580→  - Output format specification\n   581→  - Key statistics\n   582→- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n   583→- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n   584→\n   585→**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n   586→\n   587→---\n   588→\n   589→## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n   590→\n   591→**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. data\n   843→- **Trial alignment**: Align trials to meaningful events (stimulus onset, movement, etc.)\n   844→- **Time windows**: Choose appropriate pre/post-event windows\n   845→- **Neuron Do this BEFORE exploring any code or data. Document everything in this file as you work.\n\n2. **FOLLOW STEPS IN ORDER**: Do not skip steps. Do not proceed to step N+1 until step N is complete. Each step has \"Done when\" criteria — verify them before moving on.\n\n3. **MATCH THE REFERENCE PROCESSING WHEN APPLICABLE**: Your processing must match what's described in the reference paper and code, except where the decoder input and output specifications or training a neural decoder require otherwise. You will be assessed on the statistics and decoder accuracy of your converted data, and on whether an expert would consider each of your decisions well justified.\n\n---\n\n## Project Context\n\n- You are a computational neuroscientist. Your goal is to load and reformat data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis.\n- You need to use the **SAME** processing of the data described in the provided reference paper and code repository when applicable. This requires examining the provided paper, code, and data to understand how the data is formatted and processed, and determine how to balance this with the requirements of the new downstream analysis.\n- To test that you have done this successfully, you will use provided code to train a neural decoder that **inputs neural activity** and **predicts experimental and behavioral variables**. \n- We will assess your work in two ways. First, statistics of the converted data and decoder accuracy will be compared to those of an expert-written solution. Second, each decision you make about how to load, filter, process, align, and save the data will be compared with the decision made by an expert. A decision that differs from the expert's is acceptable if it is equally well justified; decisions that are poorly justified will be flagged as concerning or incorrect.\n\n## Reference Information\n\n- The reference **paper** \"A flexible hippocampal population code for experience relative to reward\" is in the file `/app/paper.pdf`.\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n- **Code** from the paper are in the directory `/app/code`.\n- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `/app/data`.\n- **Documentation** on nwb file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io/en/latest/\n\n## Decoder Task\n\nTemporally align based on start of the trial. \n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n- Time from start of trial in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n- Environment type (binary, ENV1 vs ENV2, per trial)\n- Trial number (continuous, per trial)\n- Previous trial outcome (binary, omitted = 0, rewarded = 1, per trial)\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n- Distance to any location in the reward zone, time-varying. Discretization bins:\n  - 0:  < -50 cm\n  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\n  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\n  - 3: 0 cm\n  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\n  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\n  - 6: > +50 cm\n- Absolute position in corridor, time-varying. Discretized into 5 equal-sized bins spanning the 450 cm track:\n  - 0: < 90 cm\n  - 1: 90 to 180 cm\n  - 2: 180 to 270 cm\n  - 3: 270 to 360 cm\n  - 4: > 360 cm\n- Speed, time-varying. Discretized into bins:\n  - 0: < 2 cm/s\n  - 1: 2-10 cm/s\n  - 2: 10-20 cm/s\n  - 3: 20-40 cm/s\n  - 4: > 40 cm/s\n- Lick, time-varying. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n- Reward zone location, per-trial. 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C\n- Reward outcome, per-trial. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the paper. \n\n**Done when**: \n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 11\" with a table of accuracies\n\n---\n\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\n\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\n\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \n\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n\n---\n\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n  - Key decisions and rationale\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n  - Validation results and tables\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n  - Dataset description\n  - How to load and use the converted data\n  - Output format specification\n  - Key statistics\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n\n---\n\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. The paper computes its own neural signal rather than using a stored one in `preprocessing.dff(F, Fneu, ..., deconvolve=True)` and stores the result as `sess.timeseries['events']`. The NWB's `Deconvolved` array is instead suite2p's own deconvolution of raw fluorescence.\n   116→\n   117→## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed? \n   118→\n   119→i. dF/F is computed from F and Fneu and then deconvolved into \"events\", by a copy of the paper's own `preprocessing.dff`. Per plane: restrict to the lap samples (or lap plus teleport, depending on the session), subtract `0.7 * Fneu`, add each trial's mean neuropil back so the ratio is a true dF/F, take a maximin baseline (Gaussian smoothing with sigma 15 samples, then a 300-sample running minimum followed by a 300-sample running maximum, the Methods' 20 s window), form `(F - baseline)/|baseline|`, smooth with a 2-sample Gaussian, and deconvolve with OASIS at `tau = 0.7` and `frame_rate/n_planes`. Cells from multiple planes are pooled afterwards.\n   120→\n   121→Whether the baseline window may span the teleport is a per-mouse, per-day fact, copied from `teleport_metadata.py`: the laser was blanked between trials except on the days listed there, where imaging continued. It matters -- on m15 day 5, spanning the teleport widens the baseline window by 35% and moves the emitted events by ~9% (median per-cell r = 0.986).\n   122→\n   123→ii.\n   124→```python\n   125→dff_curr, events_curr = dff(fluorescence_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n   126→                            pd.Series(trial_start_idx + 1), pd.Series(trial_end_idx + 1),\n   127→                            f_neu=neuropil_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n   128→                            neuropil_method='subtract', baseline_method='maximin',\n   129→                            subtract_baseline=True, neu_coef=0.7, tau=0.7,\n   130→                            frame_rate=frame_rate, n_planes=nplanes, deconvolve=True,\n   131→                            keep_teleports=keep_teleports)\n   132→```\n   133→\n   134→iii. This is the processing the Methods describe: \"baseline fluorescence was calculated within each trial independently using a maximin procedure with a 20 s sliding window ... dF/F was then calculated for each cell as the fluorescence minus the baseline, divided by the absolute value of the baseline, then smoothed with a two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel. The activity rate was extracted by deconvolving dF/F with a canonical calcium kernel using the OASIS algorithm as used in Suite2p.\" The parameters are theirs: `neu_coef = 0.7` and `baseline_method = 'maximin'` from `notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`, `tau = 0.7` from the suite2p ops in `notebooks/suite2p_notebooks/example_m12.ipynb`.\n   135→\n   136→The neural sampling rate is the same for all recordings once the multi-plane sessions are accounted for. Note that the `rate` stored on the NWB series is the scanner rate, so on the two-plane sessions it is 31 Hz and the per-plane rate -- the one that sets both the time bin and the deconvolution kernel -- is `rate/nplanes`.\n   137→\n   138→## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n   139→\n   140→i. Two filters, both the paper's. Cells are first restricted to the `iscell` ROIs, which carry suite2p's manual curation. Putative interneurons are then dropped: any cell whose dF/F correlates with the animal's running speed at r > 0.5.\n   141→\n   142→ii. \n   143→```python\n   144→iscell = np.array(roi_data['iscell'].to_list())[:,0] == 1\n   145→fluorescence.append(fluorescence_curr[:,iscell])\n   146→neuropil.append(neuropil_curr[:,iscell])\n   147→...\n   148→isint = is_putative_interneuron(dff_curr, speed)\n   149→spike_data.append(events_curr[~isint].T)\n   150→```\n   151→\n   152→iii. `iscell` is the manual curation the Methods describe. The per-session counts approximately matches ranges in the paper. The second filter is the Methods' additional step of filtering putative interneurons. \n   153→\n   154→## 2-d. The initial timestamp for the trial is subtracted. \n   195→\n   196→ii. \n   197→```python\n   198→behavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series\n   199→timestamps = behavior_data['trial number'].timestamps[:] \n   200→for trial in range(ntrials):\n   201→    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n   202→    timestamps_curr = timestamps[idx]\n   203→    ...\n   204→    input_curr[0] = timestamps_curr - timestamps_curr[0]\n   205→```\n   206→\n   207→iii. Common sense\n   208→\n   209→## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from start of trial in seconds* aligned with the neural data? \n   210→\n   211→i. Neural and behavioral data is already temporally aligned in the stored data, nothing needed to be done. A check was made that the number of time points was the same in the neural and behavioral data, and cropped to the shortest if they did not match\n   212→\n   213→ii. N/A\n   214→\n   215→iii. Data rates for the neural and behavior data were the same, and all offsets were 0. \n   216→\n   217→## 4-a. From inspection, this environment variable is constant in the trial and can only be 0 or 1, which matches the ENV1, ENV2 variable description in the paper. \n   232→\n   233→## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Environment type*?\n   234→\n   235→i. None\n   236→\n   237→ii. N/A\n   238→\n   239→iii. N/A\n   240→\n   241→## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Trial number* derived from?\n   242→\n   243→i. Trial number is the within-session trial index, derived from the loop counter over trials. The trial boundaries themselves come from the `trial_start` and `teleport` behavior time series.\n   244→\n   245→ii.\n   246→```python\n   247→for trial in range(ntrials):\n   248→    ...\n   249→    input_curr[2] = trial\n   250→```\n   251→\n   252→iii. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Previous trial outcome* derived from?\n   266→\n   267→i. Derived from the `Reward` behavior time series. Reward event timestamps are matched to behavior timestamps, and a binary `isreward` array marks timepoints where rewards occurred.\n   268→\n   269→ii.\n   270→```python\n   271→reward_amounts = behavior_data['Reward'].data[:][:T]\n   272→reward_times = behavior_data['Reward'].timestamps[:]\n   273→reward_time_indices = np.searchsorted(timestamps, reward_times)\n   274→isreward = np.zeros(T)\n   275→isreward[reward_time_indices] = 1\n   276→```\n   277→\n   278→iii. The `Reward` time series has its own timestamps (not aligned to the behavior sampling rate), so `searchsorted` is used to find the nearest timepoint. An assertion checks that the alignment error is within half a time bin.\n   279→\n   280→## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Previous trial outcome*?\n   281→\n   282→i. For each trial, check whether any reward event occurred in the *previous* trial's time range. For the first trial, set to 0. The value is constant across all timepoints within a trial.\n   283→\n   284→ii.\n   285→```python\n   286→if trial == 0:\n   287→    input_curr[3,:] = 0\n   288→else:\n   289→    prev_reward_idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial-1], trial_end_idx[trial-1], dtype=int)\n   290→    isprevreward = np.any(isreward[prev_reward_idx])\n   291→    input_curr[3,:] = int(isprevreward)\n   292→```\n   293→\n   294→iii. The instructions specify previous trial outcome as binary (omitted=0, rewarded=1). The code checks if any reward event fell within the previous trial's time boundaries.\n   295→\n   296→## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n   297→\n   298→i. Derived from the `position` behavior time series and the reward zone location for the current trial. The reward zone boundaries come from the `reward_zone` behavior time series. This variable is non-zero when the mouse is in the reward zone. I combine this with the position of the mouse when this is non-zero to figure out the closest reward zone. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \n   299→\n   300→ii. Assigning reward zone location for each trial: \n   301→- Before converting, the `survey()` function was used to try to understand all the data values, including whatever is going on with the `reward_zone` variable. It first computes the position of the min and max position of the mouse when `reward_zone` is non-zero:\n   302→```python\n   303→behavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series       \n   304→info['reward_zone_positions'] = np.full((ntrials, 2), np.nan)\n   305→position = behavior_data['position'].data[:]\n   306→for trial in range(ntrials):\n   307→    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n   308→    pos_trial = position[idx]\n   309→    reward_zone_trial = reward_zone[idx] > 0\n   310→    if not np.any(reward_zone_trial):\n   311→        continue\n   312→    info['reward_zone_positions'][trial] = [np.min(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial]), np.max(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial])]\n   313→```\n   314→The function `segment_reward_positions()` uses the Viterbi algorithm to assign reward zone labels so that the initial rewarded positions are close to the corresponding rewarded zone:\n   315→```python\n   316→reward_zone_dict = {'A': [80, 130],\n   317→                    'B': [200, 250],\n   318→                    'C': [320, 370]}\n   319→...\n   320→sigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\n   321→zone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\n   322→dist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n   323→                    startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\n   324→dist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\n   325→log_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n   326→```\n   327→It also encourages the reward zone label to not change often:\n   328→```python\n   329→pstay = .9\n   330→log_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\n   331→np.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n   332→```\n   333→\n   334→iii. The paper defines reward zones A, B, C at specific position ranges. These same ranges could also be found, with some translation, in the code (required mapping X -> A, etc.). I plotted the position of the mouse when `reward_zone` was positive (note that the value was between 0 and 6 I think) to determine that the Viterbi approach would likely work, and that the start of the rewarded position was the least noisy variable to use. The class fractions were approximately 1/3 after this, so it seemed correct. \n   335→\n   336→## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n   337→\n   338→i. For each timepoint, compute the signed distance from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the reward zone. Distance is 0 when inside the zone, negative when before the zone, and positive when past it.  The continuous distance is then discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n   339→\n   340→ii.\n   341→```python\n   342→def compute_distance_to_reward_zone(position_curr, reward_zone_curr):\n   343→    ntimepoints = len(position_curr)\n   344→    reward_zone_range = reward_zone_dict[reward_zone_curr]\n   345→    distance_to_reward_zone = np.zeros(ntimepoints)\n   346→    idx_before_zone = position_curr < reward_zone_range[0]\n   347→    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_before_zone] = position_curr[idx_before_zone] - reward_zone_range[0]\n   348→    idx_after_zone = position_curr > reward_zone_range[1]\n   349→    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_after_zone] = position_curr[idx_after_zone] - reward_zone_range[1]\n   350→    return distance_to_reward_zone\n   351→\n   352→```\n   353→```python\n   354→distance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n   355→...\n   356→output_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n   357→```\n   358→\n   359→\n   360→iii. This matches the paper's concept of distance relative to the reward zone. The reward zone boundaries are from `reward_zone_dict`, inspired by the reference code `Sosa_et_al_2024/src/reward_relative/behavior.py`. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n   361→\n   362→## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n   363→\n   364→i. The continuous distance is discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n   365→\n   366→ii.\n   367→```python\n   368→distance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n   369→...\n   370→output_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n   371→```\n   372→\n   373→iii. The bin edges match the instructions. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n   374→\n   375→## 7-d. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* aligned with the neural data?\n   376→\n   377→i. The position data and neural data share the same time indices within each trial, so no additional alignment is needed.\n   378→\n   379→ii.\n   380→```python\n   381→idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n   382→spike_data_curr = spike_data[idx]\n   383→position_curr = position[idx]\n   384→```\n   385→\n   386→iii. Discretized into 5 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, 90, 180, 270, 360, inf]`, corresponding to 90 cm wide bins spanning the 450 cm track. Within the converted trials the position ranges from -0.8 to 451.8 cm, so the open first and last bins absorb the few samples that fall just outside the track (185 of 1,307,665). \n   405→\n   406→ii.\n   407→```python\n   408→position_curr = position[idx]\n   409→output_curr[1] = np.digitize(position_curr, position_bins) - 1\n   410→```\n   411→\n   412→```python\n   413→position_bins = [-np.inf,90,180,270,360,np.inf]\n   414→...\n   415→output_curr[1] = np.digitize(position_curr, position_bins) - 1\n   416→```\n   417→\n   418→\n   419→iii. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n   525→\n   526→i. Several cases are handled:\n   527→- **Neural/behavior length mismatch**: If the number of neural time bins differs from behavior timestamps, data is cropped to the minimum of the two with a warning printed.\n   528→- **Short trials**: Trials with fewer than 50 timepoints (`min_ntimepoints`) are skipped with a warning.\n   529→- **Missing reward zone data**: Trials where `reward_zone` is never active (all zeros) get NaN positions, and the Viterbi algorithm handles these via uniform emission (assignment driven by neighboring trials' transitions).\n   530→- **Reward timestamp alignment**: An assertion verifies reward times align within half a time bin of behavior timestamps.\n   531→\n   532→ii.\n   533→```python\n   534→if T != len(timestamps):\n   535→    print(f\"Warning: number of neural time bins ({T}) does not match number of behavior timestamps ({len(timestamps)}), cropping to the minimum of the two\")\n   536→    T = min(T, len(timestamps))\n   537→    spike_data = spike_data[:T]\n   538→    timestamps = timestamps[:T]\n   539→...\n   540→if idx.sum() < min_ntimepoints:\n   541→    print(f\"Skipping trial {trial}...\")\n   542→    istrial[trial] = False\n   543→    continue\n   544→```\n   545→\n   546→iii. These are defensive checks found during data exploration. The neural/behavior mismatch occurs in a small number of sessions.\n   547→\n   548→## 13-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n   549→\n   550→i. The most time-consuming steps are:\n   551→1. **Loading NWB files** (`pynwb.NWBHDF5IO` and reading large arrays) — I/O bound\n   552→2. **The survey step** — loads every NWB file to gather statistics and reward zone positions\n   553→3. **Full conversion** — loads every NWB file again and extracts all trial data\n   554→4. **Saving the .pkl file**\n   555→\n   556→ii. N/A\n   557→\n   558→iii. The NWB files are large (contain full neural recordings). Conversion is otherwise quite fast\n   559→\n   560→## 13-b. The Viterbi inner loop (lines 503-507) iterates over states, which could be vectorized with matrix operations.\n   563→\n   564→ii. N/A\n   565→\n   566→iii. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n   569→\n   570→i. The survey step and the conversion step both load every NWB file and read the same data arrays (neural, behavior). The survey reads neural data to count neurons and check rates, then the conversion reads it again.
